paper_metadata.title: Recurrence of afebrile status epilepticus in a population-based study in Rochester, Minnesota

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a well-established population-based records-linkage system (Rochester Epidemiology Project) which captures all medical contacts for residents. The inclusion/exclusion criteria are clearly defined, and the sample represents a complete geographic cohort, minimizing selection bias.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Study subjects were all residents of Rochester, MN, identified because febrile seizure, acute symptomatic seizure, unprovoked seizure, or epilepsy was identified between 1955 and 1984.
items.reasoning: The target population is clearly defined as the residents of a specific geographic location (Rochester, MN) within a specific timeframe.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: Subjects with incident afebrile SE were ascertained through the records-linkage system of the Rochester Epidemiology Project. This system includes all contacts of Olmsted County residents with the medical system in southeastern Minnesota, including inpatient, outpatient, and home visits.
items.reasoning: The use of the Rochester Epidemiology Project records-linkage system ensures comprehensive capture of cases across all levels of care, reducing recruitment bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between January 1, 1965, and December 31, 1984.
items.reasoning: The start and end dates for the recruitment of incident cases are explicitly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: residents of Rochester, MN... southeastern Minnesota
items.reasoning: The geographic location and the medical settings (inpatient, outpatient, home visits) are clearly described.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: We defined SE as a single clinical seizure lasting more than 30 minutes or repeated seizures over a period of more than 30 minutes without intervening recovery of consciousness. We excluded seizures lasting less than 30 minutes whether or not they were stopped by valium...
items.reasoning: The study provides a precise clinical definition for inclusion and specific scenarios for exclusion (e.g., seizures <30 mins, EEG changes without clinical features).

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: This system includes all contacts of Olmsted County residents with the medical system
items.reasoning: Because this is a population-based records-linkage study rather than a voluntary recruitment study, participation is effectively 100% of identified eligible residents.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Information was collected on age, gender, duration, seizure type, etiology, therapeutic response to initial antiepileptic drug medication
items.reasoning: Key prognostic factors and demographic data are collected and reported for the baseline sample.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study accounts for censoring due to death or moving out of the area. The use of a records-linkage system allows for high-quality follow-up, and the statistical methods (Kaplan-Meier) appropriately handle censored data.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Subjects were followed until the date of last medical contact in southeastern Minnesota, the date of last southeastern Minnesota residency, or date of death.
items.reasoning: The study followed all 183 identified cases until death, migration, or the study end date, which is standard for population-based cohorts.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: ascertained though the medical records-linkage system... followed until the date of last medical contact
items.reasoning: The system automatically tracks residents across different providers, minimizing 'drop out' unless they leave the geographic area.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: date of last southeastern Minnesota residency, or date of death.
items.reasoning: The reasons for censoring (death or migration) are explicitly identified.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: This difference was not accounted for by differential mortality or loss to follow-up among males
items.reasoning: While the authors mention checking for differential loss to follow-up by gender, they do not provide a detailed table comparing all baseline characteristics of those lost to follow-up vs. those who completed follow-up.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text asserts there was no differential mortality or loss to follow-up that explained the gender findings, but data comparing 'completers' vs 'non-completers' is not explicitly presented.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While most factors are well-defined, the classification of 'therapeutic response' and 'seizure type' relied on retrospective review of medical notes from various personnel, which introduces potential for measurement error or inconsistency.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Predictors were defined as follows: Seizure type... Etiology... Duration... Age... Therapeutic response...
items.reasoning: Each prognostic factor (PF) is given a specific operational definition in the Methods section.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The classification of seizure type was based upon the description written by the attending medical staff, neurologists, nurses, and trained medical personnel
items.reasoning: The study relies on retrospective chart review of notes from various staff. While reviewed by two neurologists, the primary data source is subjective and not originally intended for research.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Duration was categorized as 30 minutes to 2 hours, 2 to 24 hours, and 24 hours or longer. Age was categorized as <1 year, 1 to 20 years, 20 to 65 years, and 65 years or more.
items.reasoning: The cut-points for age and duration are standard clinical/epidemiological categories and do not appear to be post-hoc or data-driven.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Charts of cases with any type of convulsive disorder were reviewed by two neurologists
items.reasoning: A standardized chart review process by two neurologists was applied to all identified cases.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: Table E-1 (referenced in text)
items.reasoning: The results suggest that the 183 cases had sufficient data for the multivariable model, though specific missingness per variable is not detailed.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no mention of imputation methods; the study likely used complete case analysis.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (recurrent SE) is defined identically to the initial event and captured through the same comprehensive records-linkage system, ensuring consistency and high sensitivity.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Recurrent SE was ascertained though the medical records-linkage system... followed until February 27, 1996.
items.reasoning: The outcome is defined as a recurrence of the inclusion criteria (SE >30 mins) and the follow-up period is specified.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Charts of cases... were reviewed by two neurologists to identify those with SE
items.reasoning: Expert neurologist review of medical records is a reliable method for identifying SE in a retrospective cohort.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Recurrent SE was ascertained though the medical records-linkage system.
items.reasoning: The same population-based surveillance system was used to detect outcomes for all participants.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study adjusts for several key clinical variables (age, sex, etiology, seizure type). However, it lacks data on specific medication changes or adherence during the follow-up period, which are significant confounders for seizure recurrence.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: We examined age, gender, duration of initial SE, seizure type, etiology of initial SE, and therapeutic response to antiepileptic drug medication
items.reasoning: While initial treatment response is measured, subsequent treatment (AED changes, adherence) during the follow-up period is not accounted for.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Predictors were defined as follows: [Age, Gender, Etiology, etc.]
items.reasoning: The confounders that were measured are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: classification of seizure type was based upon the description written by the attending medical staff... reviewed by two neurologists
items.reasoning: The measurement of confounders relies on the same expert-reviewed medical records as the PFs.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: For each resident with a first episode of afebrile SE... we examined the risk of recurrent SE
items.reasoning: Confounders were extracted from the same medical record system for the entire cohort.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No imputation methods are described.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study is a cohort study; confounding was not addressed in the design phase (e.g., matching).

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Cox proportional hazards regression was used to examine the effect of predictors on the risk of subsequent SE. Predictors that were significant in the univariate model were retained in the multivariate model.
items.reasoning: Multivariable Cox regression was used to adjust for significant confounders.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods (Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression) are appropriate for time-to-event data. The authors report both crude and adjusted ratios, and the results are presented transparently.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: We used Student t test to compare continuous variables... Kaplan–Meier survival analyses... Cox proportional hazards regression
items.reasoning: The analytical plan is standard and clearly described.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Predictors that were significant in the univariate model were retained in the multivariate model.
items.reasoning: The study uses a standard stepwise approach based on univariate significance.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Cox proportional hazards regression
items.reasoning: Cox regression is the appropriate model for analyzing prognostic factors in a cohort study with varying follow-up times.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table: Crude and adjusted rate ratios (RRs) and 95% CIs
items.reasoning: The table reports results for all variables considered, including those that were not statistically significant (e.g., age, duration).
